The Participants section includes recruitment sources, age, gender, inclusion and exclusion criteria, diagnostic assessment, and allocation by randomization. That gives a solid basic structure.

The strongest part is that the student includes the core subsections expected in the writing guide and provides enough information to understand the planned study at a general level. The interventions are distinguished clearly enough, and the follow-up timing is stated.

However, several important details are missing or underdeveloped, which keeps this section in the Adequate rather than Good range. For example, allocation is mentioned, but the randomization procedure itself is not described in enough detail. There is no explanation of whether allocation was concealed, whether randomization was stratified, or how many participants ended up in each group in the planned methods. Reward/compensation is mentioned, but only briefly.

In Materials, some information is placed somewhat awkwardly. The subsection mixes intervention description and procedural elements. The dependent measure LSAS-CA is described reasonably well, but not fully according to the guide: the developers and reference are given, the response format is explained, and an example is included, but scoring is somewhat unclear because the stated total range seems inconsistent with the item description. Reliability/validity is only briefly mentioned. Also, the instruction that Materials should avoid procedural phrasing is not always followed.

The Procedure section is too brief. It gives the broad chronology, but not enough detail about what participants did across sessions, how long assessments took, what happened after treatment, and how follow-up was conducted. There is also no separate Analyses subsection, even though the Results later uses a mixed ANOVA.

So overall the study design is coherent and understandable, but one or two important methodological details are missing and some information is not fully elaborated in the expected place. That fits a 6.5.
results_feedback:
The Results section contains several expected elements: there is a brief statement about the sample, an attempt at reporting assumption checks, a demographics table, a table with means and standard deviations, the main ANOVA results, post-hoc tests, and a reference to a figure. This shows that the student is following the general sample structure, which is positive.

However, the section has major completeness and reporting problems that substantially lower the grade. The most important issue is that key statistical information is missing or reported incorrectly. The F-tests do not include degrees of freedom: for example, 'F(2, )' and 'F(1, )' are incomplete. Since the rubric and sample results explicitly expect test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value, this is a substantial omission. The table formatting is also highly problematic. Table 1 does not match the expected concise demographics structure from the sample and is unnecessarily difficult to read. Table 2 is malformed to the point that the means and standard deviations are hard to interpret confidently.

There are also content inconsistencies. The procedure states a 12-month follow-up, but one sentence in the post-hoc section suddenly refers to a 'drie maanden follow-up'. That creates confusion about the actual design. In addition, the interpretation of the post-hoc findings is not fully consistent with the means: the text says the VRET+CGT group had a larger post-treatment reduction, but later also says the in vivo group continued improving at follow-up, which changes the comparative interpretation. That can be discussed, but the reporting should be clearer and more systematic.

The assumptions paragraph is also weak. It claims all assumptions were met because p-values were above .05, but does not report the actual tests, and the Greenhouse-Geisser discussion is not presented at the level expected by the sample. The figure itself is not actually shown in the submitted text, only referenced.

Because the section is relevant and shows an attempt at the expected analysis, but has one or more very poorly written or incomplete elements and misses crucial reporting details, it fits the Developing range. A 5.5 is appropriate because it is just at the threshold: the analysis is not incoherent, but the reporting is too incomplete for an Adequate score.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion has a clear opening paragraph that restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between short-term and long-term findings. That is a strong start and aligns well with the writing guide. The student does not merely repeat the hypothesis, but explicitly states that it was supported on the short term and not on the long term.

A further strength is that the student attempts to interpret each main finding separately and to compare it with earlier research. The discussion refers back to Anderson, Kampmann, and Bouchard, and it also returns to the theoretical framework by using Emotional Processing Theory and Inhibitory Learning Theory to interpret the pattern. This is exactly the kind of linking back to the introduction that the rubric values.

The limitations section is also reasonably study-specific. The issue of lack of blinding is relevant and well argued. The limitation concerning the short intervention duration is also meaningfully connected to adolescent treatment and inhibitory learning. Future research suggestions follow from the findings and limitations and are more specific than generic suggestions.

The main weakness is that some of the interpretation is not fully consistent with the reported results, and some conclusions are stronger than the results justify. For example, the student says VRET+CGT is more valuable than CGT+in vivo despite earlier acknowledging that the long-term hypothesis was not supported and that in vivo improved further at follow-up. That broader evaluative conclusion is somewhat overstated given the mixed pattern. There are also a few inaccuracies in referencing the prior studies, such as citing 'Anderson et al. (2017)' instead of the 2013 study, and some explanations remain speculative without being clearly marked as such.

In addition, the third finding paragraph partly overlaps with the first and could have been integrated more efficiently. The theoretical implications are present, but not always sharply distinguished from general interpretation. Still, the discussion is clearly more than a summary: it interprets, compares, critiques, and considers implications.

Overall this fits the Adequate-to-Good border, but because some reasoning is still somewhat uneven and a few claims are overstated, a 7.0 is the best fit.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear. All major sections are present, and the reader can follow the intended argument without major difficulty. Terminology is mostly consistent, especially around SAS, VRET, and CGT, and paragraphing is generally functional.

That said, the writing is not yet in the Good range. There are quite a few language and formatting issues throughout the paper. These include grammar and spelling problems, awkward phrasing, punctuation errors, inconsistent capitalization, missing spaces, and some APA inaccuracies in both in-text citations and the reference list. Examples include inconsistent spacing around citations, malformed journal titles and volume/page formatting, inconsistent use of initials and ampersands, and several citation errors. Some sentences are also clumsy or imprecise enough to reduce smoothness, even if they do not fully impede understanding.

There is also some redundancy, especially in the Discussion where similar points about VRET's short-term effectiveness are repeated. A few statements are vague or awkwardly formulated, and there are some inconsistencies such as SAS/SAD and follow-up timing.

Still, the language generally does not obstruct comprehension, and most paragraphs do have a main focus. Because the scientific language is satisfactory and understandable but clearly contains multiple noticeable issues in grammar, style, and APA, this fits the Adequate band. A 6.5 is therefore appropriate.

intro_feedback: De introductie heeft een duidelijke en overwegend coherente lijn van maatschappelijke relevantie naar theorie, eerdere literatuur, kennislacune, onderzoeksvraag en hypothese. De maatschappelijke relevantie staat vroeg en is goed gekoppeld aan sociale angststoornis bij adolescenten. Ook zijn de drie verplichte kernstudies (Anderson et al., 2013; Kampmann et al., 2016; Bouchard et al., 2017) en een extra relevante studie opgenomen. Sterk is dat de student expliciet motiveert waarom juist adolescenten onderzocht moeten worden en waarom een follow-up ontwerp nodig is. Daarmee voldoet de sectie goed aan de belangrijkste onderdelen uit de writing guide. Wel blijft de synthese wisselend: sommige studies worden echt als bouwstenen gebruikt, maar andere stukken zijn meer samenvattend dan argumentatief. Ook zijn er enkele inhoudelijke onnauwkeurigheden of minder sterke redeneringen, bijvoorbeeld rond de precieze werking van VRET versus CGT, en de claim dat VRET 'vooral gedragsmatig' werkt waardoor angst zou kunnen terugkomen is wat simplistisch onderbouwd. Daarnaast is de theoretische onderbouwing relevant, maar niet altijd strak gekoppeld aan de specifieke vergelijking VRET+CGT versus CGT+in vivo op lange termijn. Ondanks deze zwakkere schakels leidt de introductie wel duidelijk naar een passende onderzoeksvraag en hypothese, waardoor dit binnen de rubric in de band 'goed' valt.
methods_feedback: De methode is coherent en sluit in grote lijnen aan op de onderzoeksvraag en hypothese. De onderdelen participanten, materialen/meetinstrumenten en procedure zijn aanwezig, en de algemene opzet van een gerandomiseerd gecontroleerd onderzoek met drie meetmomenten is duidelijk. Positief is dat inclusie- en exclusiecriteria genoemd worden, randomisatie wordt vermeld, en de twee behandelcondities inhoudelijk van elkaar worden onderscheiden. Ook is het meetinstrument LSAS-CA redelijk volledig beschreven, met ontwikkelaars, doel, voorbeelditem en scoring. Toch ontbreken er een paar belangrijke details die volgens de writing guide wel verwacht worden. De manier van randomiseren wordt niet verder uitgewerkt, er staat weinig over eventuele toewijzingsprocedure of standaardisatie tussen therapeuten, en de procedure is erg summier. Er ontbreekt bijvoorbeeld meer detail over volgorde, duur van de meetmomenten, informed consent/debriefing, en hoe follow-up praktisch werd uitgevoerd. Ook staat onder 'Materialen' deels procedurele informatie, en de beschrijving van de afhankelijke meting is niet altijd helemaal nauwkeurig geformuleerd. Verder is er lichte inconsistentie in demografische informatie: in de methode worden alleen jongens en meiden genoemd, terwijl in de resultatentabel ook non-binaire deelnemers voorkomen. Dat maakt de rapportage minder strak. Al met al is de methode voor dit niveau voldoende tot goed, maar mist nog enkele belangrijke specificaties om echt sterk repliceerbaar te zijn.
results_feedback: De resultaten zijn begrijpelijk opgezet en volgen deels het voorbeeld uit de sample results: er is een korte inleiding, een demografische tabel, een beschrijving van de mixed ANOVA, rapportage van hoofd- en interactie-effecten en post-hocvergelijkingen. Dat is positief. Tegelijkertijd bevat deze sectie meerdere tekortkomingen die binnen de rubric duidelijk doorwegen. Het grootste probleem is dat de statistische rapportage onvolledig en deels inconsistent is. De vrijheidsgraden ontbreken bij alle F-toetsen, terwijl die volgens de sample en rubric expliciet gerapporteerd moeten worden. Tabel 2 is ook slordig en moeilijk leesbaar opgesteld, waardoor de gemiddelde scores en standaarddeviaties niet helder gepresenteerd worden. Verder wordt in de tekst gesproken over een 'drie maanden follow-up', terwijl het ontwerp eerder een 12-maanden follow-up noemt; dat is een inhoudelijke inconsistentie. Ook ontbreken de verwachte resultatenonderdelen op het niveau van de sample, zoals een echt nette tabelstructuur en een voldoende uitgewerkte figuurweergave. De assumptierapportage is aanwezig, maar vrij oppervlakkig en niet volledig transparant. Daarnaast sluit de interpretatie van de post-hocresultaten niet overal goed aan op de gerapporteerde gemiddelden. Voor dit niveau is dit niet onvoldoende, maar wel duidelijk onder het niveau van een gemiddelde tot goede resultatensectie. Daarom valt deze sectie in de 'developing' band.
discussion_feedback: De discussie heeft een duidelijke structuur en opent goed met het doel van het onderzoek, de hypothese en een samenvatting van de belangrijkste bevindingen. De student probeert de resultaten systematisch te koppelen aan eerdere literatuur en aan de besproken theorieën, wat duidelijk in lijn is met de rubric. Ook zijn er studiespecifieke beperkingen genoemd, zoals het gebrek aan blindering van beoordelaars, en worden concrete ideeën voor vervolgonderzoek geformuleerd. Dat zijn duidelijke pluspunten. Tegelijkertijd zijn er inhoudelijke problemen die de kwaliteit van de redenering iets verlagen. De grootste zwakte is dat de interpretatie niet altijd goed aansluit op de eigen resultaten. De discussie stelt enerzijds dat het langetermijneffect van VRET+CGT niet blijvend is, maar anderzijds dat de daling van pre- naar follow-up in die conditie groter was dan in CGT+in vivo; dat is moeilijk te rijmen met de eerder gerapporteerde gemiddelden, waarin CGT+in vivo juist verder lijkt te verbeteren op follow-up. Daardoor is de centrale interpretatie niet overal consistent. Daarnaast worden sommige verklaringen vrij stellig gebracht terwijl de data daar maar beperkt basis voor bieden, bijvoorbeeld over adolescentenontwikkeling en generalisatie naar echte sociale situaties. De koppeling aan Emotional Processing Theory en Inhibitory Learning Theory is aanwezig, maar soms wat algemeen en niet altijd scherp uitgewerkt op resultaatsniveau. Desondanks is er duidelijk sprake van echte interpretatie, verbinding met literatuur en theorie, en relevante beperkingen en implicaties. Daarmee is deze discussie gemiddeld tot licht bovengemiddeld, maar nog niet overtuigend genoeg voor de 'goed'-band.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen goed leesbaar en de globale structuur is duidelijk. De secties zijn logisch opgebouwd en de lezer kan de rode draad meestal volgen. De terminologie is meestal consistent, en de schrijver gebruikt overwegend passend wetenschappelijk taalgebruik voor dit niveau. Wel zijn er vrij veel taal- en stijlproblemen die het geheel minder sterk maken. Er zijn meerdere grammaticale en formuleringstechnische fouten, onhandige zinsconstructies, inconsequente spelling van termen en afkortingen (bijvoorbeeld SAS/SAD, LSAS-CA/LSAS-Ca), en APA-onvolkomenheden in zowel in-text citations als referentielijst. Ook zijn sommige zinnen omslachtig of net niet helder geformuleerd, en er zijn meerdere kleine slordigheden in interpunctie en opmaak. De tabellen en statistische notatie zijn daarnaast niet netjes uitgewerkt. Deze fouten maken de tekst niet onbegrijpelijk, maar zorgen er wel voor dat de stijl eerder adequaat dan sterk is. Daarom past een voldoende binnen de band 'adequate'.

intro_feedback:
The introduction shows a clear overall topic, establishes societal relevance early, and leads to a concrete research question about self-guided versus therapist-guided VRET for social anxiety. A strength is that the paper does more than just list studies: it tries to build an argument that self-guided VRET may work through increased autonomy/self-efficacy, and this does culminate in a clear hypothesis. The required core VRET literature is mentioned, and references are generally used responsibly.

The main reason this is not higher is that the line of reasoning is only somewhat convincing rather than fully convincing. The literature integration is uneven: Anderson, Kampmann, and Bouchard are grouped together, but their specific contributions to the present design are not worked out in much detail. Some claims are too broad or insufficiently tied to the exact target population and design. The theoretical framework around self-efficacy is relevant, but it remains somewhat indirect: the paper argues that self-guidance should increase self-efficacy, yet this mechanism is not measured in the proposed study, and the bridge from autonomy/self-guidance to reduced social anxiety could have been argued more tightly. In addition, the final transition to the exact design and hypothesis is present, but somewhat abrupt and not fully refined. Overall, this is a coherent and relevant introduction with a visible storyline, but it is not yet consistently strong in synthesis and justification.
methods_feedback:
The Methods section is coherent at a basic level and the design matches the stated research question: three conditions, pre-post measurement, and social anxiety as the dependent variable. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, which supports a passing score. The section also includes some important elements such as recruitment, compensation, random assignment, inclusion criteria, and a description of the intervention conditions.

However, there are several incompletenesses and inconsistencies that keep this section in the developing-to-adequate range. Participant information is missing important required details: there is no full age range summary in Participants beyond later discussion, no exclusion of specific practical issues relevant to VR, and no clear reporting of gender and age in the Participants subsection itself. The design description is somewhat confusing: the paper says social anxiety measures were taken before and after the intervention, but the exact timing and setting of assessments are not specified clearly. Allocation is described as 'using AI (coinflip),' which is not an appropriate or sufficiently professional description of randomization. The materials section is underdeveloped for the therapist-guided condition and unevenly detailed across conditions; it also omits several questionnaire details expected in the writing guide, such as an example item, score range, and cut-off explanation. Procedure also introduces analysis ('Repeated Measures ANOVA'), which belongs elsewhere. Finally, the conditions are not well standardized: the self-guided group has 14 daily sessions while the therapist-guided group has 4 sessions, so the comparison risks confounding guidance with treatment dose. So while the methods are understandable and mostly related to the RQ, they are not fully complete or well controlled.
results_feedback:
The Results section follows the expected general structure reasonably well: it starts with sample information, includes a demographics table and a table with means per condition and time point, reports the main analysis, and includes post-hoc comparisons. That gives the section a solid basic structure for this course level.

Still, there are enough reporting problems to prevent a higher grade. The statistical reporting is incomplete and sometimes inconsistent. Several test results are missing degrees of freedom formatting details and exact statistics are not reported correctly according to the sample style; for example, F values are given without full formatting and in a way that seems implausible for the stated design. There is no reporting of standard ANOVA assumptions beyond normality, even though repeated-measures analyses typically also require discussion of other assumptions where relevant. The interpretation of post-hoc results is also inconsistent: first the paper states that the post-measurement difference between conditions was significant, but then says there was no significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET at post-assessment. That could in principle both be true if the overall post-hoc pattern is driven by the waitlist comparison, but the reporting is too unclear to make that reasoning transparent. There is also a carry-over error where the text refers to 'PCL-5 scores' instead of LSAS scores, which suggests limited control over the reporting. Figure 1 is announced but not actually presented in the submitted text. Overall, the results are mostly relevant and partly complete, but the reporting quality and coherence are only moderate.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion gives a clear answer to the research question and explicitly states that both active conditions reduced social anxiety, while the hypothesis that self-guided VRET would outperform therapist-guided VRET was not supported. That is a good starting point, and the section does engage with the unexpected finding rather than ignoring it. It also connects findings back to previous literature and offers a plausible interpretation: therapist guidance may carry benefits that offset autonomy-related advantages of self-guided treatment. The section further includes relevant limitations and future research suggestions, and the conclusion stays reasonably close to the actual findings.

The section is not stronger because the interpretation remains somewhat surface-level and not fully integrated with the theoretical framework developed in the introduction. The paper invokes self-efficacy as the central explanatory mechanism, but because self-efficacy was not measured, the discussion cannot really test or refine that theory; this issue is mentioned indirectly but could have been discussed more explicitly as a theoretical limitation. The relation to the earlier VRET studies is also somewhat broad rather than carefully comparative. In addition, the discussion misses some sharper critical reflection on design-specific issues, especially the unequal treatment intensity between conditions, which is one of the most important limitations because it complicates the main comparison. The practical implications are present in the conclusion, but they are somewhat optimistic relative to the methodological weaknesses. Overall, the reasoning is correct and mostly coherent, with relevant reflection, but not yet fully complete or consistently convincing.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References are all present and easy to follow. Most paragraphs have a discernible focus, and the scientific tone is mostly appropriate for this level. This supports an adequate score.

At the same time, there are quite a few language and style issues that prevent a stronger evaluation. There are multiple awkward phrasings, grammar issues, punctuation errors, and occasional word-choice problems (for example, 'for this cause,' 'absolve a daily session,' repeated spacing/punctuation inconsistencies, and some unclear sentence constructions). APA style is inconsistent in several places, including citation formatting, spacing, capitalization, and reference formatting. There are also internal inconsistencies and editing errors, such as the incorrect mention of PCL-5 in the Results section and some imprecise statistical notation. Paragraphing is mostly functional, but some sections are somewhat repetitive and could be more concise. Overall, the writing does not seriously impede understanding, but it is clearly not near-faultless.

intro_feedback:
The introduction presents a clear topic, gives societal relevance early, defines key concepts, and ends with a clear aim and hypothesis. The overall line of reasoning is generally coherent: the paper moves from increasing social anxiety and digitalization, to VRET as an established treatment, to the gap concerning self-guided VRET, and then to the hypothesis that self-guided VRET may outperform therapist-guided VRET. That gives the introduction a recognizable hourglass structure and a relevant research question.

The strongest part is that the student does not merely list studies, but uses them to build toward the proposed comparison. The self-efficacy framework is also relevant and connected to the hypothesis, which strengthens the scientific reasoning. In addition, the required core studies are included and used responsibly.

What keeps this section from a higher grade is that the literature synthesis is only partly convincing. Some empirical descriptions are inaccurate or too broad. For example, Kampmann et al. is presented as a comparison with individual in-vivo exposure therapy, while the characterization is not fully precise, and the discussion of the three core studies remains somewhat brief and not always strategically linked as building blocks. The theory section also makes a fairly large inferential leap from autonomy/choice to self-efficacy to superior treatment effectiveness, without sufficiently addressing possible benefits of therapist guidance already in the introduction. As a result, the argument is coherent and relevant, but not fully convincing or nuanced.

Overall, this is a solid, above-average introduction for this level: clear RQ, relevant scientific gap, and a visible argumentative line, but the theoretical and empirical integration could be tighter and more precise.
methods_feedback:
The methods section describes a coherent design that matches the stated research question: a three-group comparison with pre- and post-measurement fits the aim of comparing self-guided VRET, therapist-guided VRET, and waitlist. The section includes the main subsections and gives basic information about recruitment, inclusion criteria, random assignment, interventions, and the main outcome measure.

The strengths are that the study design is understandable, the main groups are clearly described, and the procedure gives a reasonable overview of what participants experienced. The LSAS is identified and briefly described, and the interventions are differentiated enough for the reader to understand the intended manipulation.

However, several required details are missing or insufficiently specified. Participant information is incomplete: the section does not report the overall mean age and SD or group-specific demographics in the Participants subsection itself, and gender composition only appears later in the Results table. Exclusion criteria are also not fully justified, and the phrase 'no prior history or diagnosis of a clinical anxiety, depressive or psychotic disorder' is conceptually odd given that the study targets high social anxiety. Allocation is described as random, but 'using AI (coinflip)' is too vague and somewhat inappropriate in tone for a methods section. The treatment descriptions are also uneven: the therapist-guided condition is described in much more detail than the self-guided condition, making comparability between conditions less clear. Important procedural details remain vague, such as where and how post-measurement occurred, whether participants completed the LSAS online or in person, and how adherence to the 14-day self-guided intervention was monitored.

There is also some subsection mixing: analytic information appears in the Procedure section rather than being presented separately or more cleanly. Replication would be possible only at a broad level, not with strong precision.

Overall, the methods are mostly correct and reasonably coherent, but they are only nearly complete rather than fully complete, which places the section in the adequate-to-good range.
results_feedback:
The results section follows the expected overall structure reasonably well. It includes a demographics table, a table of means by condition and time, reports the main analysis, and briefly describes post-hoc comparisons. This aligns with the sample results format at a basic level and is a clear strength.

However, the section has several reporting problems that keep it from a higher grade. First, the statistical reporting is incomplete and partly inconsistent. Important test details are missing, such as full F-statistics formatting and degrees of freedom that seem implausible for the reported design. The ANOVA is labeled as repeated measures, but the degrees of freedom shown do not fit a straightforward 3 x 2 repeated-measures design, and no explanation is given. Assumption checks are too limited: only normality is reported, while other relevant assumptions are not addressed. Second, there is inconsistency in the interpretation of the post-hoc results. The student first writes that the post-measurement difference between conditions was significant and that the therapist-guided condition showed the biggest reduction, but then states there was no significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET at post-assessment. These statements can both be true if the significant effect concerns all three groups including waitlist, but this is not explained clearly enough. Third, there is a carryover error where the outcome is referred to as 'PCL-5 scores' instead of LSAS, which suggests limited control over the reporting.

In addition, the figure is announced but not actually presented in the paper text provided. The operational-level reporting is present, but only partly coherent and not fully polished.

Overall, the results are mostly relevant and largely complete for this level, but the inconsistencies and unclear statistical reporting lower confidence. This places the section around adequate rather than clearly good.
discussion_feedback:
The discussion gives a clear answer to the research question and states whether the hypothesis was supported. It correctly concludes that both intervention conditions reduced social anxiety symptoms and that the prediction of superiority for self-guided VRET was not supported. That main conclusion is consistent with the reported findings and provides a solid opening.

A strong point is that the student does not ignore the unexpected finding. The discussion explicitly addresses the absence of a significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET and offers a plausible interpretation: therapist guidance may provide compensating benefits such as support and structure. This is a meaningful attempt to interpret the findings rather than simply restating them. The section also includes relevant limitations and future directions that are at least partly study-specific, especially the issue of variability in adherence in the self-guided condition.

What limits the grade is that the discussion is somewhat narrower and less analytically developed than it could be. The paper does connect back to the self-efficacy account, but only briefly, and it does not really evaluate the theoretical framework in depth. For example, it could have discussed more explicitly whether the findings challenge the assumption that greater autonomy necessarily translates into greater efficacy, or whether self-efficacy was not actually tested because it was never measured. The link back to the introduction's broader societal relevance is also relatively brief and mostly deferred to the final conclusion. In addition, some interpretations rely on outside studies comparing guided and self-guided interventions in somewhat different contexts, which is acceptable, but the paper could more clearly separate speculation from direct evidence.

Overall, this is a coherent and relevant discussion with a correct main conclusion, reasonable interpretation, and meaningful limitations. It is above average, though not fully complete or deeply integrated at the theoretical level.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and understandable, with a recognizable scientific structure and mostly appropriate academic tone. Most sections and paragraphs have a clear topic, and the reader can generally follow the argument from introduction to conclusion. This supports a passing to average-above-average score for language and style.

At the same time, there are quite a few language and APA issues that prevent a higher grade. There are grammar and wording problems such as awkward phrasing ('had to absolve a daily self-administered VRE session,' 'partook,' 'for this cause'), punctuation problems, inconsistent capitalization, and some sentence-level clumsiness. Referencing is mostly responsible, but APA style is inconsistent: for example, spacing and punctuation around citations vary, some in-text citations are formatted awkwardly, and reference formatting is not consistently APA. There are also some notable clarity issues and imprecisions, such as the strange date on the title page, inconsistent terminology (SA vs SAD), and the PCL-5 slip in the Results. Some redundancy is present, especially where findings are repeated across the Discussion and Conclusion.

Overall, the language does not impede understanding, but it is not polished. The paper fits best in the adequate range: mostly clear and structured, with several noticeable grammar, style, and APA errors.

intro_feedback:
The introduction has a clear topic, a recognizable research question, and a generally coherent line toward the hypothesis. The societal relevance is present early and the paper defines key concepts such as social anxiety, VRET, and self-efficacy. The student also uses the required core literature and adds additional articles relevant to self-guided interventions, which supports the scientific relevance of the comparison. A strength is that the paper does more than merely list studies: it uses prior work to motivate why self-guided VRET might be worth testing.

At the same time, the argumentation is only somewhat convincing rather than fully strong. The hourglass structure is visible, but the reasoning has some important weaknesses. The discussion of the three core studies is too brief and partly inaccurate: for example, the studies are not always characterized carefully in relation to the proposed design, and their specific contribution as building blocks toward this exact research question remains underdeveloped. The theoretical framework around self-efficacy is promising, but the paper makes a fairly large inferential step from autonomy/choice to higher self-efficacy to superior symptom reduction, without sufficiently integrating direct empirical evidence that this mechanism applies in self-guided VRET for social anxiety. In addition, the final transition to the exact aim, hypothesis, and design is present but not especially sharp or concise.

Overall, this fits the rubric level of adequate to good: the reasoning is correct and coherent, the RQ is clear and relevant, and references are used responsibly, but the literature synthesis and theoretical justification are not yet fully convincing enough for a higher score.
methods_feedback:
The method section describes a coherent three-group design that is related to the stated research question and hypothesis. The main components—participants, materials, and procedure—are all present, and the general setup is understandable for this student level. The inclusion criterion based on LSAS is given, random assignment is mentioned, the reward is reported, and the intervention conditions are described in broad terms.

However, the section is only nearly complete rather than fully complete and correct. Several details that the writing guide expects are missing or too vague. Participant characteristics are incomplete in the Participants section itself: no mean age, SD, or gender distribution are reported there, only later in the Results table. Exclusion criteria are underdeveloped and somewhat oddly phrased (e.g., no prior history or diagnosis of anxiety/depressive/psychotic disorder is not well justified for a study on social anxiety symptoms). The allocation procedure is not described professionally enough: 'using AI (coinflip)' is unclear and raises questions about actual randomization. The design timing is also somewhat confusing, because the self-guided condition receives daily sessions for 14 days, whereas the therapist-guided condition receives only 4 sessions over the same period; this difference is substantial and should have been justified more explicitly as part of the manipulation rather than left implicit. 

The materials description is also uneven. The LSAS is described only partially: there is no example item, no score range, and no explanation of cutoffs beyond eligibility. The intervention descriptions are not equally detailed across conditions, making comparability difficult. The therapist-guided condition seems focused mainly on public speaking scenarios, whereas the self-guided condition includes a broader range of social situations; this creates a possible confound that is not acknowledged in the Methods. In the Procedure, analysis information is included ('we then used statistical analysis...'), which belongs more naturally in a separate analysis subsection.

Sommige verklaringen zijn vrij speculatief en worden vrij stellig gebracht, bijvoorbeeld dat VRET toegankelijker is en deelnemers daardoor ervaringen beter blijven toepassen in het dagelijks leven; dat is plausibel, maar in deze studie niet direct gemeten. Daarnaast is de vergelijking met eerdere literatuur aanwezig maar nog niet overal even precies; Anderson et al. wordt bijvoorbeeld genoemd als steun voor korte-termijneffecten, maar de verschillen in design worden niet steeds diep besproken. Toch is dit over het geheel een goede discussie: coherent, relevant en duidelijk verbonden aan de introductie.
